name: Sunlight treatment (heliotherapy)

card.summary: Controlled sun exposure used since antiquity and popularised in the early 1900s to treat disease, and still used in clinics for skin conditions such as psoriasis that affect how skin looks.
card.note: UV exposure damages skin and is linked to skin cancer; modern use is supervised.

quick.overview:
Heliotherapy is the therapeutic use of sunlight. In the early twentieth century physicians such as Auguste Rollier prescribed graduated sun exposure at mountain clinics for tuberculosis and other illnesses. Today the approach survives mainly as supervised climate or sun therapy for skin conditions, notably psoriasis, which can clear or lighten visible plaques.

Appearance benefits come through the skin: a randomised trial of a four-week supervised course found a clear immediate improvement in psoriasis, with about half the patients still better six months later. Sunlight also supports vitamin D production, and tanning has been fashionable since the 1920s.
quick.how: Historically, patients were exposed to sun in stages under medical supervision, often at altitude. Modern programmes send patients with skin disease to sunny locations such as Gran Canaria for supervised exposure of a few weeks. Narrowband UVB lamps in clinics are a related, controlled form.
quick.risks: UV light causes progressive skin damage, sunburn and is linked to skin cancer and cataracts. The WHO, American Cancer Society and US Surgeon General have issued warnings about UV exposure. Photosensitising drugs, some herbs and conditions such as porphyria increase risk.

lead: Heliotherapy is the medical use of sunlight. Ancient Greek, Egyptian and Roman cultures practised it, and Indian texts from around 1500 BCE combined herbs with sunlight for pale patches of skin.[4] In the early twentieth century it became a mainstream cure: Niels Finsen won the 1903 Nobel Prize for light treatment of skin tuberculosis, and Auguste Rollier opened an Institute of Heliotherapy at Leysin in 1903, later running clinics with more than 1,000 beds.[4][5]

For people interested in appearance, the live use is skin. Supervised sun exposure is used for psoriasis, and phototherapy more broadly for vitiligo and atopic dermatitis, which change how visible skin looks.[1][2][4] Sun also drives vitamin D production, and tanned skin became fashionable in the 1920s.[6]

In the UK light therapy was mainstream from the late 1800s to the early 1930s, until controlled trials by Dora Colebrook found it ineffective for the wide range of conditions it had been used for.[4] Tuberculosis heliotherapy ended once antibiotics arrived in the 1940s.[3][5]

chain: UV immune and pigment effects in skin
angle.text: Sunlight exposure can reduce visible psoriasis in supervised courses and, through UV, can darken skin. Both effects change how skin looks, and both carry UV-related skin-damage risk.

infobox: UV skin damage and skin cancer

paras: Finsen, a Faroese physician, treated lupus vulgaris with concentrated light and is regarded as the father of modern phototherapy.[4] Rollier (1874-1954) opened his Leysin institute in 1903, combined sun with fresh air, rest and altitude, and treated skeletal tuberculosis; he wrote La Cure de Soleil in 1914.[5] Reported figures after World War I claimed 1,746 of 2,167 patients recovered under his care.[5]

Before tuberculosis chemotherapy began in 1944, management relied on aerotherapy, heliotherapy and nutrition, as in the Swiss mountain resorts depicted in Thomas Mann's The Magic Mountain.[3] A 1917 article in the Canadian Medical Association Journal discussed the method.[7]

Heliotherapy and climatotherapy remain in use for chronic skin disease.[8][2] Narrowband UVB phototherapy is the most commonly used form for children, and heliotherapy is among modalities reviewed for psoriasis, vitiligo and atopic dermatitis.[2]

Early sun exposure causes rapid immune changes in the skin and blood of psoriasis patients, according to a study of twenty patients exposed on Gran Canaria.[9] Sun also acts through vitamin D and through other UV pathways, including tanning.[1]

A randomised cross-over trial of 95 psoriasis patients given a four-week supervised heliotherapy course found a highly significant immediate improvement; about half still had reduced psoriasis six months later and about a quarter at one year.[10] Another study examined sun exposure and vitamin D, glucose and lipids in psoriasis patients during climate therapy on Gran Canaria.[11] A 2024 randomised trial tested heliotherapy against standard care for newborn jaundice.[12] Heliotherapy for acne is not established; blue and blue-red light show moderate evidence for mild acne, mostly in low-quality studies.[4]

UV causes progressive skin damage, sunburn and erythema, and is linked to collagen damage, cataracts and skin cancer.[4] A 2010 study linked frequent tanning-bed use to roughly triple the risk of melanoma.[6] Risk is greater with photosensitising drugs, St. John's wort and conditions such as porphyria.[4]

timeline.event: Finsen wins the Nobel Prize; Rollier opens Leysin institute.[4][5]
Rollier publishes La Cure de Soleil.[5]
Controlled trials by Colebrook question wide use of light therapy.[4]
Streptomycin begins the era of tuberculosis chemotherapy.[3]
